backups.overview: Mount Stone is a high-prominence, triple-summited peak (South/main summit 6,612 ft, plus Middle ~6,600 ft and North ~6,400 ft summits) above Lake of the Angels in the southeastern Olympic Mountains. It is the highest point in Mason County. The lower approach lies in the Mount Skokomish Wilderness (Olympic National Forest); the upper basin, lake, and summit sit just inside the Olympic National Park boundary. On a clear day the summit gives views of The Brothers, Mount Washington, Mount Anderson, Mount Constance, Mount Deception, and Mount Olympus.
backups.beta: From Hamma Hamma River Road, hike the steep Putvin Trail (FST 813) through Olympic National Forest gaining nearly 3,000 feet in less than 4 miles. Emerge in an alpine basin at Lake of the Angels (~4,900 feet), then traverse along the base of the cliffs short of St. Peter's Gate to a notch in the West Ridge, then scramble Class 3 up the ridge with some exposed class 4 moves to reach the South Peak summit.
backups.turnaround: Manage afternoon weather; the scramble itself has no fixed crux to gate, but loose rock warrants care.
backups.comms: Cell phone coverage is unreliable or absent in the alpine basin and summit area; do not depend on cellular service. A satellite messenger (Garmin InReach, SPOT) is strongly recommended for emergency communication. Alert someone of your plan and expected return time before starting the hike.
backups.descent: Reverse the south slopes back to Lake of the Angels.
obj_haz: Steep snow/ice on approach slopes into early summer

backups.detailed_rack: Helmets are essential due to loose Olympic basalt and rockfall hazard. Ice axes recommended for travel June-July when snow and ice patches are common. Microspikes useful for frozen snow. Trekking poles recommended for steep descent on Putvin Trail.

Backpack (20-25L for day hike, 40L+ for overnight)

Carry an ice axe before late July — the St. Peter's Gate saddle holds snow/ice well into summer

watch_out: Some parties rate the summit-block moves class 4, not class 3 — be prepared to downclimb the same terrain

backups.pro_needs: Rock scrambling experience, comfortable with exposure, navigation skills (map, compass, GPS). Helmets recommended due to rockfall hazard and loose rock common to Olympic basalt.
backups.best_season: Late July through September is most reliable; the headwall gully and St. Peter's Gate saddle can hold snow/ice into July, and the Hood Canal convergence zone can bring afternoon cloud or showers even in midsummer.
backups.approach: From the Putvin Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road (FS 25, ~1,600 ft), the Putvin Trail (#813) is a steep, primitive trail, unmaintained in its upper reaches, that climbs steeply and directly from the start — expect root-staircase steps and a boot-track tread through forest for the first mile. About halfway up, the trail meets a rock headwall that requires hand-over-hand climbing; a large tree root serves as the key handhold, and on at least one especially steep pitch a fixed handline rope has historically been in place to assist. Above the headwall the trail eases into subalpine forest and heather meadows, passing near Whitehorse Basin and the Pond of the False Prophet before reaching Lake of the Angels (~4,850 ft) in a dramatic cirque below Mt. Stone's south face and the St. Peter's Gate notch — about 3 miles and roughly 3,000 ft of gain from the road. There is little to no reliable water on the lower trail; carry enough to reach the lake, and expect the trail to be slick when wet and to hold snow on shaded steps into early summer. From the lake, contour/climb toward St. Peter's Gate; just before the gate, turn sharply left (south) and traverse along the base of the cliffs to a notch in Mt. Stone's west ridge. Turn right at the notch and climb directly toward it, arriving at a first sub-summit rock; climb a short, low-Class-3 chimney to its top, cross a brief, somewhat exposed ridge to the base of the true summit spire, then follow a groove in the rock on the left side that bends right, where a faint climbers' path leads the last steps to the summit. The route is Class 3, with a few moves on the summit block that some parties rate Class 4 (rated Grade I in the Olympic Mountains climbing guide); from Lake of the Angels camp, figure roughly 2.5 hours up to the summit.
backups.descent_text: Descend by reversing the same west-ridge/south-face scramble line back through the summit groove, exposed ridge, and chimney to the notch, then retrace the cliff-base traverse back to Lake of the Angels — allow roughly 1.5 hours summit-to-camp per the Olympic Mountains climbing guide. From Lake of the Angels, descend the Putvin Trail the way you came: the rock headwall (tree-root handhold, sometimes a fixed handline) and the trail's many steep, loose, root-braided sections are noticeably harder on tired legs headed downhill — face-in downclimbing at the headwall and trekking poles on the lower switchbacks are both recommended. This is a walk-off/scramble descent on the standard route; no rappelling is required anywhere on the climb or the trail, and no fixed rappel anchors exist on this line.
backups.bail: Retreat to Lake of the Angels is straightforward from the slopes.

pitch_detail.notes: An unmaintained, very steep climbers' trail from Hamma Hamma River Road that climbs roughly 3,000 ft in about 3 miles to Lake of the Angels. Carry water: the lower trail is largely dry, and roots and steps are slick when wet.

Midway up, the trail meets a rock headwall climbed hand over hand on roots, sometimes with a fixed handline. Above it a climbers' path leads to a small meadow near 4,400 ft. Downclimb it facing in on the way out.
Continue north from the meadow and the lake toward St. Peter's Gate, the notch in the ridge above the basin. This ground can stay snow-covered into summer.

Just before the Gate, turn sharply left (south) and traverse along the base of the cliffs to a notch in the west ridge. Parties who lose the faint path here are drawn up into steeper Class 3–4 gullies on the south face; stay with the cliff base.

Turn right at the notch and scramble a couple of hundred feet to a first sub-summit, finishing up a short low-Class-3 chimney. Beyond it, a shallow hanging basin with a small lingering snowfield leads across toward the summit block.

A short, somewhat exposed ridge reaches the base of the summit spire. Climb the groove on its left side, which bends right, then a faint path to the top; the rock is solid pillow basalt, with a few Class 4 moves reported. Reverse the same line to descend.

approach_variants.name: Putvin Trail from Hamma Hamma Road to Lake of the Angels
approach_variants.notes:
From the Putvin Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road (FS 25) at about 1,565-1,600 ft — an unmarked roadside pullout, roughly 4.5 miles past the Lena Lake Trailhead — the Putvin Trail is an unmaintained, primitive user trail that climbs steeply and directly from the first steps. Expect root-staircase steps and boot-track tread through forest for the first mile. In recent years a slide near road mile 10.5 has at times blocked the last 1.2 miles of road, adding a road-walk; check Forest Service status.

About halfway up the trail meets a rock headwall requiring hand-over-hand climbing, with a large tree root as the key handhold and, historically, a fixed handline on the steepest pitch. Above it the trail eases into subalpine forest and heather meadows, passing near Whitehorse Basin and the Pond of the False Prophet, and reaches Lake of the Angels at roughly 4,850-4,920 ft in a cirque below Mount Stone's south face — about 3 to 3.5 miles and 3,000 ft of gain. Little to no reliable water on the lower trail; carry enough to reach the lake.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Snow lingers in the basin above the lake well into summer
hazards: Trail-less, route-finding-dependent terrain above Lake of the Angels
Near-vertical root and rock steps on the lower Putvin Trail, genuinely exposed when wet, and worse descending on tired legs
Loose rock on the headwall and summit block with rockfall onto parties below
An ambiguous Class 3/4 crux near the summit
Fog is common here and multiple parties have lost the route on the upper mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS A NOTCH IN MOUNT STONE'S WEST RIDGE, AND THE TEST FOR IT IS A TURN YOU MAKE BEFORE A GATE. From Lake of the Angels contour and climb toward ST. PETER'S GATE — the obvious notch above the basin. JUST BEFORE THE GATE, TURN SHARPLY LEFT (SOUTH) and traverse along the BASE OF THE CLIFFS to a notch in the west ridge. If you walk through St. Peter's Gate, you have gone too far; the Gate is the marker you turn short of, not the one you pass through. That works in cloud because the cliff base is a tactile handrail: once you have made the turn, you keep rock on one side of you the whole traverse. Lose contact with the cliff and you have drifted downhill. SECOND TEST, at the notch: turn RIGHT and climb toward a first sub-summit rock, then up a short LOW CLASS 3 CHIMNEY to its top. A chimney is a shape you can feel with both hands. If the first difficulty above the notch is a face or a slab rather than a chimney you can bridge, you are not on the line. THIRD TEST, on the summit spire: from the sub-summit cross a brief, somewhat exposed ridge to the base of the true summit spire, then follow a GROOVE on the LEFT side that BENDS RIGHT, where a faint climbers' path leads the last steps to the top. Left then right — a groove that runs straight up is not it. WHAT THE ROUTE'S OWN TIMING SAYS: about 2.5 hours up from the Lake of the Angels camp and about 1.5 hours back down. If you have been on the ground above the lake far longer than that without finding the notch, you have most likely missed the turn short of the Gate. FOG WARNING SPECIFIC TO THIS MOUNTAIN: Mount Stone has more than one summit, and parties have confused the true south summit with the Middle and North summits in cloud. Count your ridges.

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake and Upper Lena Lake, the St. Peter's traverse from the east
approach_variants.notes:
The other side of the same notch. From the Lena Lake Trailhead on FS 25 at roughly 600-750 ft, take the well-graded Lena Lake Trail #810 about 3 miles to Lena Lake at about 1,800 ft, then the steep primitive tread up the West Fork Lena Creek drainage roughly 3.5 more miles to Upper Lena Lake at about 4,550 ft, some 6.5 miles and 4,000 ft from the trailhead. Upper Lena Lake is the last maintained-trail camp and the last reliable water before the traverse goes cross-country; wilderness permit and bear canister required.

From Upper Lena Lake, leave the trail and head west on the Scout Lake way-trail across meadows and heather past Lena Tarn to Scout Pass at about 5,200 ft, down slightly to Upper Scout Lake, round it into Scout Basin, and up to Ullin's Pass at about 5,000 ft above the tarns known as Ullin's Bathtubs. From there a rising traverse above the small lakes leads to a snow ramp across a steep hillside below Mount Stone that ends at a loose moraine, and then exposed dirt-and-mud slopes to St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft.

This is a two- or three-day trip and it is chosen for the country it crosses, not because it is quicker.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the off-trail benches and passes are largely clear
hazards: Extensive off-trail way-trail route-finding over multiple passes and basins with faint tread
Loose glacial moraine of all sizes near St. Peter's Gate and exposed dirt-and-mud slopes on the final ramp
Fog on the upper mountain — multiple parties have lost the route here and ended up in harder terrain
No dependable water between Upper Lena Lake and the tarns near Ullin's Pass
A very long approach with limited bail options partway through
approach_variants.baseFinding: COMING FROM THE EAST YOU ARRIVE AT ST. PETER'S GATE ITSELF, WHICH IS THE HIGH POINT OF THE TRAVERSE AT ABOUT 5,950 FT AND AN OBVIOUS ROCKY NOTCH IN MOUNT STONE'S SOUTHEAST RIDGE. That is the arrival test and it is unmistakable in any weather: the ground stops rising, the notch pinches, and the Lake of the Angels basin opens on the far side. FROM THE GATE THERE ARE TWO WAYS ONTO THE PEAK AND THEY ARE DIFFERENT CLIMBS. The one this route describes is the west-ridge notch: go THROUGH the Gate and drop toward the Lake of the Angels basin, then work back up and turn the corner onto the cliff-base traverse to the notch in the WEST ridge — the same notch the Putvin parties reach by turning sharply left just short of the Gate. The other is the south-face gully, which starts by descending about 300 ft from the Gate to the base of a basalt cliff; that is the Lena Lake traverse route's line, not this one. SO THE FOG TEST FOR THIS VARIANT IS WHICH SIDE OF THE GATE YOU END UP ON: this route goes over to the Lake of the Angels side and approaches the west ridge from the south-west, keeping the cliff base at your shoulder. ABOVE THE NOTCH THE TESTS ARE IDENTICAL to the Putvin variant: turn right, low Class 3 CHIMNEY to a sub-summit, a brief exposed ridge, then a GROOVE on the LEFT that BENDS RIGHT to the true south summit.

bivy.name: Lake of the Angels
bivy.notes: The base for Mount Skokomish and for the south side of Mount Stone, and one of the best-placed camps in the Olympics for a climber. About 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft from the Putvin trailhead, which understates it badly — the trail is notoriously steep, with hand-over-hand sections on rock and root where a slip has real consequence, and it is slow going with an overnight pack. From the basin the east slopes of Mount Skokomish are a straightforward scramble, and Mount Stone is gained by working north toward St. Peter's Gate, so a fit party can take both peaks in one day from these tents. The four sites and the meadow are the constraint: this is a fragile alpine basin that has been loved hard, so camp only on the designated ground and expect company. Best from mid-July, once the steep upper trail is clear of snow, through September. Early season the last pitch to the basin holds snow and the trail is genuinely hazardous when wet.
bivy.water: The lake, but READ THIS ONE CAREFULLY. It is a shallow basin lake fed by snowmelt with no significant inlet, so it draws down through the summer and by a dry late season it can be low, warm and unappealing, and the meadow seeps around it disappear entirely. There is a good spring roughly two miles up the Putvin trail that is often the last dependable water on a dry year. Late-season parties should plan to carry water up from lower on the trail rather than count on finding it in the basin
bivy.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED — the trail crosses the park boundary shortly before the final climb into the basin, having already passed through the Mount Skokomish Wilderness on Forest Service ground below. Book through Recreation.gov or obtain the permit from a park wilderness information office; per-person nightly fees apply. An animal-resistant food container is required. NO CAMPFIRES — the basin is far above the 3,500 ft fire limit and this is stove-only ground. No dogs. No Northwest Forest Pass or other parking pass is needed at the Putvin trailhead itself, which is unusual for this road and worth knowing
bivy.capacity: Four designated sites in the upper basin. Four. It is a small hanging meadow and there is no overflow ground that is acceptable to camp on

bivy.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a CONTINGENCY AND STAGING SITE RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
bivy.water: NO POTABLE WATER AT EITHER CAMPGROUND — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
bivy.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
bivy.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

backups.overview: Mount Seattle (6,246 ft) rises deep in the Olympic interior, about 7.5 miles southeast of Mount Olympus, within the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park. Its northeast aspect drops over 3,800 ft to the Elwha valley in only about 1.5 miles, but the standard scramble routes stay on the gentler south/west scree and talus slopes. The peak was named April 29, 1890 by James Halbold Christie and topographer Charles Adams Barnes of the Seattle Press Expedition, in honor of the city that sponsored their winter crossing of the range; it was first climbed in 1907 by Asahel Curtis, Grant Humes, and Lorenz Nelson while reconnoitering for a climbing club's first attempt on Mount Olympus. Reaching the base of the peak requires a long, committing wilderness approach from either the Elwha or North Fork Quinault drainages — there is no easy day-trip line to this summit.
backups.beta: Most parties base-camp at Seattle Meadows (~4,550 ft), reached via a multi-day approach up the North Fork Quinault River to Low Divide and then west into Seattle Creek Basin. From camp, climb scree slopes on the mountain's western side, cross over a ridge, and continue up scree and talus on the eastern side, finishing with a class 2-3 scramble on the east ridge/side to the craggy summit. Two other approach variants exist (via Noyes Basin, and a more direct line up Seattle Creek Basin itself), converging on the same upper-mountain scramble.
backups.turnaround: Because the upper mountain is loose scree/talus with real rockfall and slip potential, and the approach is long and entirely off-trail through remote wilderness, set a firm turnaround time before starting the summit push and commit to it — visibility loss (fog/cloud) on the unmarked upper slopes is the biggest threat to a safe descent, and there is no faster way down than the way up.

backups.pro_needs: No technical protection is documented for this route — it is an unroped Class 3 scramble with no glacier travel per the published route description.
backups.approach: Two realistic approach corridors exist, both multi-day: (1) North Fork Quinault side — from the North Fork Quinault Trailhead at the end of the North Shore Road (not the South Shore Road, which leads to Graves Creek and the East Fork instead), follow the North Fork Quinault River Trail or the higher, rougher Skyline Ridge Primitive Trail (via Three Lakes and Kimta Peak) to Low Divide, roughly 16-20 miles one-way depending on the line chosen, then cross-country/climbers'-path to Seattle Meadows below the peak's south side. (2) Elwha side — from the Whiskey Bend trailhead (the road to it has been closed to vehicles at Madison Falls since November 2017 flood damage, adding about seven miles each way on foot or bike), follow the Elwha River Trail up the Elwha valley toward Elwha Basin/Low Divide (on the order of 20+ miles one-way), then leave trail to climb into Seattle Creek Basin or Noyes Basin on the peak's northeast side. Either way, plan on a multi-day backpack just to reach a base camp, with several thousand feet of trail gain before any scrambling begins. The Seattle Creek Basin approach (Elwha side) follows the creek's waterfalls until the drainage steepens, forcing a steep, brushy bushwhack up onto the Mt. Noyes-Mt. Seattle ridge — expect slow going in heavy brush low down.
backups.descent_text: Descend the ascent line in reverse: downclimb the east ridge scramble back to the scree/talus on the east side, cross back over the connecting ridge, and descend the west-side scree to Seattle Meadows camp. The scree and talus are loose and unconsolidated in places, so downclimb carefully rather than trying to glissade or boot-ski except where lingering early-season snow makes it safe; rockfall onto parties below is a real concern on the looser sections.
backups.bail: Reverse the scramble; no fixed anchors required.

access.rules: Hard-sided, approved bear-resistant food canisters are required for all overnight stays throughout most of Olympic Wilderness, including the Elwha and Quinault interior zones; bear wires/hangs are not accepted. approach_variants.baseFinding: The staging point is Seattle Meadows, the high camp in upper Seattle Basin about a thousand feet above Seattle Creek. There is no gully mouth to find here: from camp the climb starts on scree on the mountain's western side, and the base is simply where meadow gives way to loose scree and the slope steepens. What identifies the route is the sequence, so hold it in mind — climb the west-side scree, cross over a connecting ridge, then continue up scree and talus on the eastern side, and finish with Class 2 to 3 scrambling on the east ridge to a craggy top. If you are still high on the west side and the ground is cliffing out above you, you have failed to make the crossing and need to traverse. The summit is confirmed by an unusually large plastic tube jammed into a crack holding the register. Coming instead up Seattle Creek Basin, follow the creek's waterfalls until the drainage steepens, then take the steep brushy bushwhack onto the Noyes–Seattle ridge; that brush low down is the crux of that variant, not the scrambling above.

bivy.name: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
bivy.notes: Low Divide is the saddle between MOUNT SEATTLE and MOUNT CHRISTIE and the obvious base for both, and by all accounts it is the most comfortable camp in the interior — flat, watered, with a toilet and a bear hang. Mount Seattle has three established scramble lines from here, by Noyes Basin, by Seattle Creek Basin and by the south slopes, and the upper meadows above camp are open walking. Mount Christie is usually taken by dropping to Martins Park, a boulder garden about three miles below the Christie Glacier, and climbing the north couloir from there. The honest planning point is which side you walk in from: this is 28.4 miles from Whiskey Bend up the Elwha, and 16 miles from the North Fork Quinault trailhead, so unless you are traversing the range you should be coming from the Quinault. Wasps have been a real problem on the lower forest sections in late summer, and stings there have put people out of action for days.
bivy.water: Reliable — a stream runs through the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not itself a quota area, but it is a long way from any road and may not appear in an online search, so telephone the wilderness information centre if the site will not show. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

bivy.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
bivy.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for MOUNT NORTON: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
bivy.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

bivy.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
bivy.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT MEANY, MOUNT NOYES, MOUNT QUEETS and MOUNT WILDER, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE HIGH Y-JUNCTION IN THE APPROACH GULLY IS THE DECISION POINT, AND THIS ROUTE TAKES THE LEFT FORK. That is a countable, binary choice on the ground, and every south-face route on this peak depends on it.

SO THE SEQUENCE IS: roughly TWO MILES south along the creek, then CROSS, then up a prominent gully to a Y, then LEFT. Crossing after half a mile instead of two puts you on the West Face approach, on the other side of the mountain, in a broad shallow gully with a chockstone in it.

ARRIVAL AT THE WALL: the base of the SOUTH FACE. The Beckey-Tate's obvious CENTRAL RAMP-AND-LEDGE SYSTEM SPLITTING THE FACE is the reference feature here, because two other routes are measured from this one and from that ramp.

HOW THE SOUTH FACE STARTS SORT OUT, IN ORDER, AND THE ONE MEASUREMENT THAT SEPARATES THEM: SKINNY START IS ABOUT 30 METRES RIGHT OF THE STANDARD KEARNEY-THOMAS START. GOING DOWN UNDER starts from the Beckey-Tate base and traverses RIGHT ACROSS OVERLAPS to its own ledge. THE CENTRAL RAMP IS BECKEY-TATE. SO: IF YOU HAVE WALKED THIRTY METRES RIGHT OF WHERE YOU MEANT TO BE, YOU ARE ON SKINNY START.

WATER IS UNRELIABLE LATE SEASON. Carry it from the creek before crossing, since the crossing is the last of it.

DESCENT: as with the neighbouring Beckey-Tate line, scramble to the notch just north of the true summit and follow the loose scree-and-snow gully back down toward the Hairpin pullout, roughly two hours from the top.

pitch_detail.notes: Starts on a nondescript crack about 40 ft down and right of the giant chockstone-filled chimney; sustained thin liebacking/stemming leads to a two-piece fixed nut-and-cam anchor on a small ledge with trees.
Double incipient cracks pull to a stellar final move; flared jams, awkward stances, and fiddly small gear make this the route's redpoint crux.
A short, easy connector pitch -- an awkward opening move off the double seams eases quickly to easier ground.
A balancy opening move leads into fun, moderate climbing through a giant hollow flake and a beautiful right-facing corner to a ledge belay.
Easier climbing trends right toward the South Arete, then rises in a traverse into the notch below the summit; belay mid-pitch to keep rope drag manageable on this long, wandering pitch.
A short final scramble tops out on the summit block -- watch for mountain goats known to frequent the summit.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START IS ROUGHLY 40 FT DOWN AND RIGHT OF THE LARGE CHOCKSTONE-FILLED CHIMNEY BETWEEN THE TWO SPIRE FORMATIONS, ON A NONDESCRIPT CRACK THAT LEADS TO A TWO-PIECE FIXED ANCHOR ON A PEDESTAL.

SO THE CONFIRMATION IS AT THE TOP OF PITCH ONE, NOT AT THE BOTTOM, AND THAT IS THE HONEST WAY TO USE THIS ROUTE: the crack itself is described as NONDESCRIPT, which means you will not identify it by looking at it. What you can identify is where it ends. A ROPE LENGTH UP, THERE IS A TWO-PIECE FIXED ANCHOR ON A PEDESTAL. If you arrive at a stance with no fixed gear, come down and move along the wall.

PITCH TWO GIVES A SECOND CONFIRMATION: OBVIOUS DOUBLE INCIPIENT CRACKS leading up to a series of ledges. Two thin parallel cracks, not one.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE TWO NEIGHBOURS, AND THE MEASUREMENTS ARE THE POINT: MOJO RISING is ABOUT 20 FT DOWNHILL of the chimney on an OBVIOUS BOLTED FACE. The NORTHWEST FACE, Boving-Pollock, is entered by TRAVERSING INTO A STEEP CORNER. THIS ROUTE IS 40 FT DOWN AND RIGHT ON A PLAIN CRACK. Bolts mean Mojo Rising; a corner means Boving-Pollock; a plain crack forty feet right of the chimney means Free Mojo.

RETREAT FROM LOW ON THE ROUTE IS STRAIGHTFORWARD, WHICH IS WORTH KNOWING WHEN YOU ARE UNSURE OF THE START: a party retreating from the fixed anchor atop pitch 1 rappels to the ground; above it the belays are built from gear, so retreating higher means leaving gear. There is no penalty for starting, finding the ground wrong, and coming back down.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE HAS NO GROUND START, AND THAT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT FACT ABOUT FINDING IT. You reach it by climbing THE FIRST THREE PITCHES OF THE SOUTHWEST RIB, or alternatively by the Northwest Face Boving-Pollock line, and THEN GOING LEFT AT A LEDGE WHERE THE TWO ROOFS COME INTO VIEW.

SO THE BASE OF THE DAY IS THE BASE OF THE SOUTHWEST RIB, AND THAT HAS A LANDMARK YOU CAN STAND UNDER: THE Y-SHAPED LARCH TREE AT THE BASE OF THE SOUTHWEST RIB, LEFT OF THE SOUTHWEST COULOIR. A larch with a forked trunk, at the foot of a rib, with a couloir to its right. That is the aiming point from the basin.

THE IN-ROUTE TEST IS VISUAL AND BINARY: GO LEFT AT THE LEDGE WHERE THE TWO ROOFS COME INTO VIEW. Two roofs, stacked. If you can see only one overhang, or none, you have not reached the ledge. If you have climbed more than three pitches of the rib you have gone past it.

A HAZARD RIGHT AT THE START OF THE PITCH, RECORDED BECAUSE IT IS EXACTLY WHERE A PARTY IS COMMITTING: THERE IS A LOOSE BLOCK RIGHT AT THE START OF THE ROOF PITCH.

WHAT NOBODY DOES HERE, WHICH ANSWERS THE OBVIOUS QUESTION: parties do not reverse this pitch. Rappelling back through an overhanging roof is awkward and is not the documented practice. Most continue up the remaining Southwest Rib pitches to the true summit and take the standard South Arete descent, downclimbing the arete to the RABBIT EARS then three single-rope 60 m rappels from bolted anchors down the gully.
